# Man-in-the-Middle Attack

A class of attack in which the attacker sits **between** two communicating parties, relaying traffic
while both believe they are talking directly to each other. Once positioned, the attacker can read,
modify, delay or drop anything that passes. Lab 08 of
[[cybersecurity-engineering-laboratories]] performs one end to end inside a lab network.

## The two halves

Every MitM has a **positioning** step and an **exploitation** step, and they are independent problems.
Positioning is the hard part; once achieved, exploitation is ordinary traffic handling.

Positioning techniques the labs enumerate:

| Technique | Layer | Why it works |
|---|---|---|
| **Wi-Fi eavesdropping** (rogue AP) | link | clients associate to a familiar SSID with no mutual authentication |
| **ARP poisoning** | link | **ARP has no authentication at all** — an unsolicited reply is believed |
| **DNS spoofing / cache poisoning** | application | name→address answers are accepted without origin authentication |
| **ICMP redirects** | network | routers are instructed to reroute a victim's traffic |
| **Port stealing** | link | the switch's forwarding table is rewritten so frames arrive at the attacker's port |
| **STP mangling** | link | the attacker's bridge claims to be the spanning-tree root |

Every one of these is a **missing-authentication** bug in a protocol designed when the local network
was assumed friendly. That is the transferable lesson: the vulnerability is not an implementation
defect anywhere, it is an omitted requirement that was reasonable in 1982 and is not now.

## What the lab demonstrated

ARP poisoning combined with DNS spoofing against a deliberately vulnerable web application on a
Metasploitable VM, with the resulting traffic captured in [[wireshark]] — showing that credentials
submitted over an unencrypted form are readable in full by the interposed host. The captured material
is **not reproduced anywhere in this wiki**; the finding is that plaintext form submission over a
network an attacker can position on offers zero confidentiality, which is the point of the exercise.

## The cryptographic form of the same attack

Lab 05 lists MitM among the classical attack models: the attacker terminates two separate encrypted
sessions, one with each party, and re-encrypts between them. Both endpoints see a valid session.
Unauthenticated Diffie–Hellman is the textbook victim — key *agreement* without key *authentication*
agrees a key with whoever is on the wire, and the report names this as DH's main risk. See
[[symmetric-vs-asymmetric-cryptography]].

## The defence is authentication, not encryption

Encryption alone does not help — the attacker simply negotiates with each side separately. What
defeats MitM is binding the far end's key to an identity you can verify:

- **[[public-key-infrastructure]]** and certificate validation for TLS: the chain is checked against a
  trust store before key agreement completes. Signing the DH exchange is precisely the fix — see
  [[digital-signatures]].
- **Channel confidentiality below the application**, verified by capture. Lab 09 captures a VPN's
  tunnel interface against the underlying one to confirm what an interposed observer can and cannot
  read.
- **Link-layer hygiene** for the positioning half: dynamic ARP inspection, DHCP snooping, port
  security, 802.1X. These do not make the protocols authenticated; they make the switch refuse the
  lie.

A proxy that intercepts your own browser traffic is the same technique used cooperatively — the lab
reports note that [[owasp-zap]] and Burp are structurally a MitM where the tester holds both roles.
That framing is worth keeping: the mechanism is neutral; only the consent differs.

## Scope

Performed in 2022 against lab VMs and deliberately vulnerable targets provided for the purpose. No
step-by-step procedure, tool invocation or captured credential from these labs appears in this wiki.
